claims.text: A supervised machine-learning model can integrate alloy composition, microstructural disorder, and atomistic phonon-scattering descriptors.
The proposed model will predict lattice thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys more accurately than traditional empirical or physics-based models.
High-entropy alloys relevant to thermal insulation exhibit multicomponent chemical disorder and significant lattice distortion.
Phonon scattering dominates lattice thermal transport in the proposed alloys over 300–700 K.
Intrinsic lattice distortions caused by multielement mixing enhance phonon scattering.
Fluctuations in interatomic force constants in a chemically disordered high-entropy alloy contribute to phonon scattering and attenuation.
Combining chemical-complexity and phonon-scattering features allows a machine-learning model to capture multiscale thermal-transport effects.
Traditional thermal-conductivity models oversimplify the multiscale effects of disorder in high-entropy alloys.
Structural disorder reduces phonon group velocities.
Structural disorder shortens phonon relaxation times.
The model will reduce prediction error by approximately 20–30% relative to traditional models.
The model will correctly identify high-entropy alloys with lattice thermal conductivity below approximately 1 W m−1 K−1.
Debye/Callaway models and empirical correlations have larger prediction errors for disordered high-entropy alloys than the proposed model.
The model's predictive improvement will apply primarily to high-entropy alloys with substantial configurational disorder and lattice distortion.
Model accuracy will diminish for minimally disordered alloys or outside the temperature regime dominated by phonon scattering.
The exact percentage reduction in prediction error cannot be established until comprehensive training data are available.
Variability in microstructural measurements and simulation-derived descriptors introduces uncertainty into the predictions.
